question_text: A 39-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist for a routine visit. She has no complaints during this visit. She had an abnormal pap test 6 years ago that showed atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. The sample was negative for human papillomavirus. On her follow-up Pap test 3 years later, there was no abnormality. The latest pap test results show atypical glandular cells with reactive changes in the cervical epithelium. The gynecologist decides to perform a colposcopy, and some changes are noted in this study of the cervical epithelium. The biopsy shows dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 39-year-old woman presents to her gynecologist for a routine visit. She has no complaints during this visit. She had an abnormal pap test 6 years ago that showed atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. The sample was negative for human papillomavirus. On her follow-up Pap test 3 years later, there was no abnormality. The latest pap test results show atypical glandular cells with reactive changes in the cervical epithelium. The gynecologist decides to perform a colposcopy, and some changes are noted in this study of the cervical epithelium. The biopsy shows dysplastic changes in the epithelial cells. Which of the following is the next best step in the management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Loop electrosurgical excision procedure
opb. Cold knife conization
opc. Follow-up pap smear in one year
opd. Follow-up pap smear in 3 years
ope. Repeat colposcopy in 6 months

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient has a history of atypical glandular cells and a biopsy confirming dysplastic changes, indicating an increased risk for cervical cancer. Current management guidelines recommend excisional procedures for patients with atypical glandular cells and dysplasia, as follow-up Pap smears are insufficient for definitive management. The Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure (LEEP) is indicated in this scenario, as it allows for both diagnosis and treatment. Evidence supports that LEEP is a preferred option in cases of dysplastic changes, aligning with the consensus that follow-up Pap smears or repeat colposcopy are inadequate in this context.
